variants.name: net/http middleware chain (Handler wrapping)
variants.implementation_notes: Go's standard library is the canonical realization: the `Handler` interface (`ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request)`) is the handler contract, `HandlerFunc` adapts an ordinary function to it, and middleware is just a function `func(http.Handler) http.Handler` that wraps the next handler, calling `next.ServeHTTP(w, r)` to forward or writing a response to stop. The framework supplies no pipeline object, so the chain is assembled explicitly (helper chains or manual wrapping), which keeps order visible in the code. Go 1.7 is the practical floor because middleware passes per-request values through the request's `context`.
pitfalls: A middleware that forgets next.ServeHTTP silently swallows the request, and a nil next panics; always terminate the chain with a real handler.
Response headers written before an inner handler runs cannot be undone, and writing after the handler corrupts the body - check before writing.
Values threaded through the request context are untyped and unenforced; key collisions and forgotten keys surface only at runtime.

variants.name: gRPC unary/stream interceptor chain
variants.implementation_notes: For RPC rather than HTTP routes, gRPC interceptors are the same pattern over typed calls: a `UnaryServerInterceptor` receives the context, the request, the call info and the `handler` (its successor), and `grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor(a, b, c)` composes several interceptors with the first as the outermost link. Prefer this variant when the request object is an RPC; the middleware reading still holds, since an interceptor either calls `handler(ctx, req)` or returns a status error, which stops the chain.
pitfalls: Chain order is invisible at the call site - the first interceptor passed is the outermost, so recovery must come first and authorisation before business handlers.
Interceptors run for streaming setup as well as unary calls; expensive checks block the whole chain, so keep them bounded.
Returning an error stops the chain but returning a nil response with a nil error confuses clients; always return a typed status error.
